title: Scalable generation of heralded single photons via active feed-forward switching of a fiber delay line
authors: Xavier Barcons Planas, Helen M. Chrzanowski, Janik Wolters
abstract: Quasi-deterministic single-photon generation is a key requirement for many photonic quantum technologies. Photon sources based on spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) are widely used for producing high-quality photons; however, the probabilistic nature of the process limits the generation of synchronized multi-photon states. Here, we demonstrate temporal synchronization of multiple photon-generation events using a free-space-fiber hybrid delay line with feed-forward control, enabling fast and efficient switching and scalable operation. Narrow-band, telecom-wavelength photons compatible for fiber transmission are heralded from a monolithic cavity SPDC source and synchronized across 20 time bins. This yields a sixfold enhancement in synchronized rates and enables multi-photon synchronization, with only a marginal increase of higher-order photon-number contributions.
summary: The paper presents an experimental demonstration of enhancing single-photon source rates by temporally multiplexing multiple photon emission events using a hybrid free-space-fiber delay line. By implementing active feed-forward switching, the system achieves significant rate enhancements (up to 180-fold for three photons) while maintaining high fidelity in the heralded signal stream.
main_problem: The core challenge is achieving quasi-deterministic single-photon generation at high count rates, synchronized to an external clock, which is essential for scaling photonic quantum technologies.
main_result: The authors demonstrated temporal synchronization of multiple heralded photon-generation events across up to 20 time bins, leading to significant rate enhancements (e.g., 180-fold for three photons) compared to non-multiplexed sources.
method: The technique employs a free-space-fiber hybrid delay line combined with active feed-forward switching triggered by the detection of an idler photon to store and release signal photons on demand.
model_or_system: The system utilizes a monolithic cavity Spontaneous Parametric Down-Conversion (SPDC) source producing narrow-band, telecom-wavelength photons. The temporal multiplexing is achieved using a delay line incorporating fiber and a free-space section controlled by a Pockels cell and polarizing beamsplitter.
key_observables: 1-photon detection rate ($R_1$), heralded second-order autocorrelation $g^{(2)}_h(0)$, and the enhancement factor for $n$-photon rates ($E_n$).
important_parameters: The cycle transmission ($\eta_c$) was measured to be 89%; synchronization is demonstrated across up to 20 time bins.
main_assumptions: Rate enhancement formulas are assumed valid in the low gain regime where multi-pair contributions are minimized; performance scaling is limited by engineering constraints.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the concept diagram of photon multiplexing, the experimental setup involving the cavity source and delay line components, measured coherence time vs. delay cycles, and rate/contamination measurements comparing multiplexed versus non-multiplexed operation.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from introducing the need for deterministic sources to detailing the hybrid free-space-fiber architecture, presenting experimental characterization of component efficiencies, demonstrating the synchronization mechanism via feed-forward control, and finally quantifying the rate enhancement achieved through temporal multiplexing.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a critical bottleneck in quantum networking: generating high-rate, synchronized entangled or heralded photon pairs. The use of active feedback to engineer time-domain resources is highly relevant for building scalable photonic quantum repeaters or sources.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. (a) Concept of photon synchronization via multiplexing (MUX) using a free-space-fiber hybrid switchable delay line. Telecom and narrow-band photons heralded from a photon-pair source are stored in the system using a free-space electro-optic switch and released at clock-synchronized time bins. (b) Experimental setup based on the concept presented in (a), in which the optical switch is implemented by combining a polarizing beamsplitter with a Pockels cell. Narrow-band telecom photons are generated via SPDC in a monolithic cavity [6] and synchronized with the fiber delay line. HWP: half-wave plate; PBS: polarizing beamsplitter; PC: Pockels cell; EPG: electrical pulse generator; SNSPD:...

FIG. 2. Measured 1-photon detection rate R1 as a function of the mean photon number per pulse µ and the number of multi- plexed time bins N. The marker color encodes the measured higher-order photon-number contributions. Both quantities are defined as cumulative over N for a fixed µ (g(2) h (0) as a weighted average), indicating the marginal increase of g(2) h (0) with multiplexing, whereas the multiplexed rate is enhanced by approximately one order of magnitude. The surface points are described by the theory (Eq. 1 for n = 1).

FIG. 3. (a) Measured n-photon detection rates Rn, and (b) measured multi-photon contamination g(2) h (0) as a function of the mean photon number per pulse µ for multiplexed (MUX, solid dark lines) and non-multiplexed (NMUX, dashed light lines) configurations. The theoretically predicted n-photon rates (Eq. 1) are overlaid in (a), and a linear regression is ap- plied to the data points in (b). The integration time for each data point is 10 (20) min for MUX (NMUX) configurations. The error bars are derived from Poissonian photon counting statistics.
